theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Fitting one ceiling light takes 45 minutes. How many hours do 8 lights take?
What word means giving a task to another team member while staying responsible for it?
What is the short talk at the start of the day, where the team leader gives out tasks and hazards, called?
What do we call extra time built into a plan to cover small delays?
A job has 30 outlets. The team fits 12 on Monday. What percentage of the outlets is done?
What device, used with a padlock, stops a breaker being switched on while work is done?
A team starts at 7:00 a.m. and works 8 hours, with a 1-hour lunch break. At what time does it finish?
What is the label fixed at an isolated switch, saying who is working and why, called?
What document records the safe conditions agreed before work in a client's plant room?
Four electricians each need 2 boxes of screws for the day, and the team leader adds 2 spare boxes. How many boxes are loaded?
When a team leader writes a SMART objective for the crew, what does its letter 'A' stand for?
Name the instrument, checked on a proving unit, that an electrician uses to prove a circuit dead. (two words)
What word means the order in which tasks are done?
A job of 64 person-hours is shared equally by a team of 4. How many hours does each person work?
What is the process of comparing what was done with what was planned, so the next plan is better, called?

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and organise a day's work for a team of four electricians rewiring part of an occupied office.
essays.modelAnswer: The day before, I would read the drawings, check the revision and agree with the supervisor and the office manager which rooms we will do and when the power can be off. I would set a clear objective, such as 'first fix rooms 3 and 4, inspected by 4 p.m.'. I would list the tasks, estimate the time for each, including set-up, isolation, testing and clear-up, and put them in a sensible order, grouped by area. I would share the tasks out by each person's skill, pairing the trainee with an experienced electrician. I would check the materials, tools and test instruments, and charge batteries. On the day I would brief the team on the tasks, hazards and isolation plan, set up barriers and signs, and track progress at midday. At the end I would record what was done and plan the next day.
markingPoints: Checks drawings and agrees areas and shutdown times with supervisor and client
Sets a clear, measurable objective
Lists, times and sequences the tasks
Allocates by skill; prepares materials, tools and instruments
Briefs, sets up safely, tracks progress and records the day

essays.stem: Explain how you would decide the order of priority for a list of jobs that includes an emergency, a deadline and routine work. Use electrical examples.
essays.modelAnswer: I would look at each job and ask two questions: how urgent is it, and how important is it? Anything that is a danger to people comes first, for example a damaged cable or a burning smell from an outlet: I would make it safe straight away by isolating and locking off the circuit. Next come jobs that are both urgent and important, such as restoring power to a clinic's vaccine fridge, or work that must be done before a fixed deadline like the government inspection. Then come important jobs that are not urgent, such as planning next month's training or servicing the test instruments, which I would schedule so they are not forgotten. Routine tasks, such as tidying the van or filing, fill the gaps. I would agree the order with my supervisor, tell the team, and review it if something new comes in.
markingPoints: Judges each job by urgency and importance
Danger to people first, made safe by isolation
Urgent and important next, with example
Important not urgent are scheduled; routine fills gaps
Agrees the order with the supervisor, tells the team, reviews when things change

essays.stem: Explain how you would give out tasks to a team with different skills and experience, and how you would check the work.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by knowing my team: each person's training, experience and what they are allowed to do. I would match tasks to people, so safety-critical work like terminating a board or testing goes to a competent electrician, while a trainee does simpler tasks or works alongside an experienced person to learn. I would try to share the work fairly and give people a chance to build new skills under supervision. I would explain each task clearly with a job card: what, where, the standard, the time and the hazards, and ask them to repeat it back. I would make sure they have the right tools and materials. During the day I would check progress and quality at agreed points, not just at the end. I would give feedback, praise good work and correct mistakes calmly. I remain responsible for the work I delegate, so I would sign it off only after checking it.
markingPoints: Knows each person's training, experience and authority
Matches tasks to competence; trainees supervised
Explains tasks clearly with job cards and checks understanding
Checks progress and quality at stages and gives feedback
Remains responsible and signs off after checking

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare the tools, test equipment and materials the evening before a job.
essays.modelAnswer: I would read the job list and the drawings and make a list of the materials needed for the next day, with sizes and quantities. I would check the store and the van against that list and order or collect anything short, so the team is not held up. I would check the hand tools and power tools for damage, make sure the insulated tools have no cracked handles, and charge the cordless tool batteries. I would check the voltage indicator and proving unit work, and the leads are not damaged. I would check the insulation tester and low-resistance ohmmeter are within their calibration dates. I would pack the lock-off kit with enough padlocks and tags for each worker, and the PPE, first-aid kit and fire extinguisher. Finally I would load the van safely, heavy items low and secured, and note anything missing in my plan.
markingPoints: Makes a materials list from the job and drawings
Checks stock and fixes shortages
Checks hand and power tools; charges batteries
Checks voltage indicator, proving unit and instruments in calibration
Packs lock-off kit, PPE, first aid, extinguisher; loads safely

essays.stem: Explain how safety is built into a work plan for electrical tasks, including safe isolation and permits.
essays.modelAnswer: Safety is planned before the work, not added afterwards. For each task I would look at the hazards, such as electric shock, work at height, drilling into hidden services, heat and manual handling, and write the controls in the risk assessment and method statement. The plan states which circuits must be isolated and when, and that safe isolation is used every time: switch off, lock off with each worker's own lock, fit a tag, and prove dead with a voltage indicator checked on a proving unit before and after. No work is done live. Where the client requires a permit to work, such as in a plant room, I would arrange it while planning, so it is ready on the day. The plan also covers PPE, barriers and signs, ladders, first aid and the emergency plan. I would brief the team on all of this before work starts.
markingPoints: Hazards identified and controls written in risk assessment and method statement
Plan states which circuits are isolated and when
Safe isolation steps every time; no live work
Permits arranged during planning
PPE, barriers, access, first aid, emergency plan; team briefed

essays.stem: Describe how you would organise a work area in a client's building so that the work is safe and efficient.
essays.modelAnswer: I would agree the work area with the client and keep it as small as the work allows. I would put up barriers and signs to keep staff and visitors out, and keep exits, walkways and fire equipment clear. I would choose one place for tools and one for materials, close to the work, so nobody walks back and forth or trips over them. Cable drums and conduit lengths would be laid where they do not block anything. I would protect the client's floors and furniture with sheets. Power for tools would come from a safe supply, with leads routed off walkways. Steps and towers would be set on firm, level ground. Waste and offcuts would go straight into bags or bins, and copper kept apart for recycling. At the end of each day I would tidy, cover any open boxes, lock away tools and leave the area safe.
markingPoints: Agrees and limits the area; barriers and signs
Keeps exits, walkways and fire equipment clear
Sets tool and material points close to the work; protects client property
Safe tool power and access equipment
Controls waste and leaves the area safe each day

essays.stem: At midday on a lighting job your team is behind its plan. Explain the methods you use to follow a team's progress through a working day, and the actions you would take to recover.
essays.modelAnswer: I would set clear targets in the morning, such as the number of rooms first fixed or outlets fitted and inspected, and mark them on a simple task board. I would check progress at set times, for example at break, lunch and mid-afternoon, by looking at the work and talking to each person. I would compare what is done with what was planned. If the team fell behind, I would find out why first: a missing part, a hidden problem in the wall, a task harder than expected, or someone needing help. Then I would act: move people to help, change the order of tasks, get the missing material, or reduce the target. I would not let anyone skip safety steps or testing to catch up. I would tell the supervisor early, with the reason and a realistic new time, and record it in the daily report.
markingPoints: Sets clear daily targets and records them
Checks progress at set times against the plan
Finds the cause of the delay
Takes action without cutting safety or testing
Tells the supervisor early and records it

essays.stem: Rain, a late delivery and a sick worker all affect the same day. Explain how you would change the plan and who you would tell.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first look at what can and cannot be done safely today. Because of the rain I would stop outdoor work such as trenching and outdoor cable runs, and move the team to indoor tasks planned for later in the week. For the late delivery, I would check which tasks need those materials, contact the supplier for a delivery time and plan tasks that can go ahead with the stock we have. For the sick worker, I would check that the remaining team still has the right skills for each task, especially any isolation or testing, and pair people so nobody works beyond their competence. I would not attempt a planned shutdown if we are too short of people to do it safely. I would write the new plan, brief the team, and tell my supervisor and the client what has changed and how it affects the finish date.
markingPoints: Stops unsafe outdoor work and moves to indoor tasks
Re-plans around the late delivery and chases the supplier
Checks skills after the absence; no one beyond their competence
Does not attempt unsafe work, such as a short-staffed shutdown
Briefs the team and tells the supervisor and client

essays.stem: Explain how you would coordinate your team's plan with other trades and with the client in a building that is in use.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the week starts I would get the builder's or client's programme and see which other trades are working in the same areas. I would talk to their leaders, agree who works where and when, and agree routes for cables, pipes and ducts so we do not clash. I would agree with the client which rooms can be used, the hours we can work, where we can store materials and when power can be switched off, giving them notice so they can protect their computers and staff. I would put these agreements in writing and on the plan. Each day I would check in with the other trades and the client's contact person, tell them of any change, and listen to their concerns. When something changes, I would update the plan and confirm it with everyone affected. Clear, regular contact prevents delays, damage and accidents.
markingPoints: Gets the programme and identifies other trades in the area
Agrees areas, times and routes with other trades
Agrees access, hours, storage and shutdowns with the client, with notice
Records agreements and checks in daily
Updates and confirms changes with everyone affected

essays.stem: Explain how you would review a week's work and use the results to plan better next week.
essays.modelAnswer: At the end of the week I would gather the daily reports, the task board, the timesheets and any inspection results. I would compare the planned and actual times for each task and see which tasks took longer or shorter, and why. I would look at problems: late materials, rework found at inspection, near misses, or waiting for other trades. I would hold a short meeting with the team, ask what helped and what got in the way, and listen to their ideas. Then I would decide on a few changes: for example, allow more time for terminating boards, order materials earlier, or add a check before second fix. I would update my estimates with the real times, so next week's plan is more realistic. I would record the lessons and tell my supervisor, and check the following week whether the changes worked.
markingPoints: Gathers reports, timesheets and inspection results
Compares planned and actual times and finds reasons
Asks the team for views and ideas
Decides changes and updates estimates
Records lessons, informs the supervisor and checks the effect

practical1.title: Plan, brief and re-plan a team's day on a multi-room training installation
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a job pack: three training bays set up as three rooms of an occupied office, the drawings, a list of tasks with their materials, an urgent fault report (a damaged cable in one room), the times the 'client' allows power to be off, and the team's skills. As a team leader group, produce: (1) a clear objective for the day; (2) a prioritised task list with times, including set-up, isolation, testing and clear-up; (3) a task allocation chart by skill, with trainees paired; (4) a materials and tools list with the checks to be made on the voltage indicator and test instruments; (5) an isolation plan for each bay; and (6) a task board for tracking progress. One member then gives a five-minute briefing to the others and the assessor. Halfway through, the assessor hands the group a change card (for example, a late delivery and a worker off sick). The group re-plans, a different member briefs the changes, and the group writes a short end-of-day report. Each member leads at least one part. Photograph each stage.
materials: Job pack from the assessor: drawings, task list, fault report, shutdown times and team skills
Flip chart or whiteboard for the task board, sticky notes and markers
Planning forms: task list, allocation chart, isolation plan, daily report
Calculators, pens and a phone or camera for photos
photos: The objective and prioritised task list
The isolation plan for each bay
The task board after the change card
checklist: Set the urgent fault as the first priority and planned to make it safe by isolation
Estimated realistic times, including set-up, isolation, testing and clear-up
Allocated tasks by skill and paired trainees with competent electricians
Planned safe isolation (off, lock, tag, prove dead with a tester checked before and after) for every bay
Re-planned sensibly after the change card without cutting safety
Briefed clearly, or helped prepare the briefing, and answered questions
Contributed accurately to the end-of-day report
safety: This is a planning task: no supply is used and no tools are needed
Plan every task so that no work is done live
Keep the room tidy, with bags and cables off the floor
Follow the Centre's rules for the classroom

practical2.title: Organise and carry out a planned installation task with progress tracking
practical2.brief: The group carries out a planned task on two of the Centre's training bays, which are never connected to a supply: a lighting circuit with two one-way switches and a socket outlet circuit, wired from a small training board to the drawing. Before starting, the group writes a short work plan with tasks, times and who does what, prepares and checks the tools, test instruments and materials against a list, and sets out the work area with barriers, a tool point and a waste point. One member leads the safe isolation of the training board (switch off, lock off, tag, prove dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after) while the others watch and check. The group then does the work, updating a progress chart every 30 minutes against the plan. Members take turns to act as team leader for each stage. At the end the group carries out a visual inspection and dead tests, tidies and secures the area, and writes a daily report comparing planned and actual times. Only the instructor may energise anything. Photograph each stage.
materials: Two training bays and a small training board (not connected to any supply)
Drawing of the lighting and socket circuits
Cable, conduit or trunking, boxes, switches, a socket outlet, lampholders and fixings
Hand tools, insulated screwdrivers, cordless drill and bits
Lock-off kit, danger tags, voltage indicator and proving unit
Low-resistance ohmmeter or multifunction tester in calibration
Barrier tape, signs, waste bags, work plan, checklist, progress chart and daily report forms
photos: The written work plan with tasks, times and names
Tools and materials laid out and checked against the list
The work area set out with barriers, tool point and waste point
The training board locked off and tagged, and the tester being checked
The daily report with planned and actual times
checklist: Helped write a realistic plan and knew their own tasks
Checked tools, instruments and materials before starting
Helped set out a safe, efficient work area
Carried out or checked safe isolation correctly
Did their share of the work neatly and to the drawing
Updated the progress chart and acted when the team fell behind
Left the area clean and secure, and helped write the daily report
safety: The training bays are never connected to a supply; only the instructor energises anything
Prove dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after, with each member's own lock and tag
Wear safety glasses when drilling and cutting; use insulated tools in good condition
Keep leads, cables and offcuts off the floor to prevent trips
Use steps safely, with one person holding them for work above head height
